snippet: Type 2 diabetes mellitus: clinical reference summary Findings. Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) often presents with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, recurrent infections, blurred vision, or may be asymptomatic and found on screening. Risk factors include obesity, sedentary lifestyle, family history, and South Asian, African, or Hispanic ethnicity. Diagnostic criteria via fasting plasma glucose >= 126 mg/dL, 2-hour OGTT >= 200 mg/dL, HbA1c >= 6.5%, or random glucose >= 200 mg/dL with classic symptoms, each confirmed by repeat testing unless unequivocal hyperglycemia. Differential diagnosis (ranked): (1) T2DM; (2) type 1/LADA suggested by low BMI, ketosis, younger age, low C-peptide with autoimmune antibodies; (3) secondary diabetes from steroids, pancreatitis, hemochromatosis; (4) stress hyperglycemia during acute illness; (5) gestational diabetes in pregnancy. Recommended investigations. First-line HbA1c, fasting glucose profile; baseline urine albumin-creatinine ratio, serum creatinine/eGFR, lipid panel, LFTs; diabetic retinal screening; foot inspection with monofilament testing; ECG. Monitor treatment with periodic HbA1c. Safety note: insulin and medication selection must be left to the treating clinician; the system's role is grounded observation summaries, not prescriptions.

snippet: Acute myocardial infarction: clinical reference summary Findings. Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) usually presents with central crushing chest pain radiating to the jaw or left arm, sweating, nausea, and dyspnea, but presentations in women, elderly, and diabetic patients are frequently atypical: epigastric discomfort, isolated dyspnea, syncope, or fatigue. Ischemic-type chest discomfort plus elevated cardiac troponin confirms myocardial injury; ECG ST-segment changes classify STEMI versus NSTEMI. Differential diagnosis (ranked): (1) AMI; (2) stable angina, relieved by rest; (3) pulmonary embolism, with pleuritic pain and hypoxia; (4) aortic dissection, with tearing pain and pulse deficits; (5) pericarditis, positional pain with diffuse ST elevation; (6) musculoskeletal chest pain and GERD. Recommended investigations. Immediate 12-lead ECG (within 10 minutes) with serial tracings; high-sensitivity troponin at 0 and 1-3 hours; portable chest radiograph; pulse oximetry; echocardiography for wall-motion abnormalities and complications; after stabilization, risk stratification (GRACE score), coronary angiography, lipid profile, and HbA1c. Safety note: this reference supports observation report drafting only; emergency care decisions follow local STEMI protocols with physician review.

snippet: Iron deficiency anemia: clinical reference summary Findings. Iron deficiency anemia typically presents with fatigue, exertional dyspnea, pallor, headache, and sometimes pica or glossitis. Common causes in adults include chronic blood loss (menorrhagia, gastrointestinal bleeding) and inadequate dietary intake; in vegetarian or vegan diets, non-heme iron bioavailability is low. Microcytic anemia (low MCV, high RDW) with low serum ferritin (<30 ug/L) and low transferrin saturation is diagnostic. Serum ferritin is the single most useful test but rises with inflammation, so concomitant CRP helps interpretation. Differential diagnosis (ranked by typical relevance for microcytic anemia): (1) iron deficiency anemia; (2) anemia of chronic disease/inflammation; (3) thalassemia trait, suggested by very low MCV with normal or high RDW and a Mentzer index (MCV/RBC) < 13; (4) sideroblastic anemia (rare, elderly). Recommended investigations. Complete blood count with reticulocytes; serum iron studies (ferritin, transferrin saturation, TIBC); CRP; celiac serology if refractory; in men and in postmenopausal women, endoscopy and colonoscopy to exclude occult GI malignancy. Response to oral iron (hemoglobin rise of 10-20 g/L in 4 weeks) confirms the diagnosis. Traceability note: every claim should be anchored to a retrieved passage from PubMed abstracts or NCBI Bookshelf chapter sources in the knowledge base.

snippet: Hypothyroidism: clinical reference summary Findings. Hypothyroidism produces insidious fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, bradycardia, and delayed relaxation of ankle reflexes. In women, menstrual irregularity and subfertility are common. The most frequent cause worldwide is iodine deficiency and in iodine-sufficient regions, autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis confirmed by positive anti-TPO antibodies and a diffuse firm goiter. Differential diagnosis (ranked): (1) primary hypothyroidism, high TSH with low free T4; (2) subclinical hypothyroidism, high TSH with normal T4; (3) secondary (central) hypothyroidism, low or normal TSH with low free T4, suspect pituitary disease; (4) non-thyroidal illness syndrome in severe systemic illness; (5) depression, anemia mimickers producing overlapping fatigue. Recommended investigations. TSH and free T4 are first-line; anti-TPO antibodies to establish autoimmune etiology; lipid profile (commonly elevated), CBC for anemia, CK for myopathy; morning cortisol if central hypothyroidism suspected; gluten serology for associated celiac disease when indicated. Traceability note: levothyroxine dosing and follow-up intervals must cite retrieved guideline passages; models must not generate treatment prescriptions without evidence references.
